item.title: Bangladesh garment workers protesting for higher wages clash with police
item.description:
Thousands of Bangladeshi garment workers blocked a major highway and clashed with police on Monday, demanding a monthly minimum wage more than double their current pay, as protests spread across industrial hubs.

The South Asian nation of 170 million people is the world’s second-biggest garment exporter behind China, manufacturing clothes for some of the largest international brands.

Hundreds of workers in Gazipur, north of the capital Dhaka, blocked the Dhaka-Tangail highway, vandalising several vehicles, while large groups took to the streets in the Mirpur district, where police dispersed demonstrators with tear gas, AFP reporters saw.

Angry workers also set fire to a police vehicle.

The protests came despite the government’s announcement on Sunday that it would establish a wage board to review the minimum wage in the vital garment industry, which employs millions of people and generates the bulk of Bangladesh’s export earnings.

However, labour leaders say workers’ grievances extend beyond the formation of the board, citing inflation and rising household expenses.

The protesters demand a 30,000-taka monthly wage, more than double their current pay.

Workers currently earn about 13,000 taka a month, according to Kalpona Akter of the Bangladesh Centre for Workers Solidarity.

Police fired stun grenades and tear gas canisters to disperse crowds in Ashulia, a Dhaka suburb and the site of some of the country’s largest factories.

“Food prices, cooking gas and electricity bills have all gone up — the government must either bring down the prices of essential commodities or raise our wages,” said Mamum, 28, a factory worker.

Machine operator Sharmin, 24, said: “We keep the wheels of the economy turning. They must listen to us.” Home Minister Salahuddin Ahmed warned that the government was taking strong action to stop the protests.

“Those engaging in unlawful activities and conspiracies under the guise of labour movements will be tackled with an iron hand,” he said after meeting industry leaders on Monday.

‘Crack down’

However, Ahmed also said earlier Prime Minister Tarique Rahman had instructed officials after hosting an emergency cabinet meeting late on Sunday to “ensure workers’ rights and improve their living standards”.

He said Rahman had told them to make sure production and exports continued “unhindered”.

Bangladesh’s main manufacturer associations for garments and knitwear warned that “prolonged unrest could disrupt production, delay export shipments and affect Bangladesh’s commitments to international buyers”, the state-run BSS news agency said on Monday.

Kamrul Hasan, general secretary of the Ekota Garments Sramik Federation, told AFP some labour leaders had gone into hiding.

“We were not prepared for this unrest either, as the wage board has already been formed,” he said.

“But workers are now protesting over wages and other unresolved issues.”

In Ashulia, security officers chased protesters as they scattered down narrow side streets, with the choking tear gas drifting into densely packed housing where families often live crammed into single rooms.

“Police fired tear gas shells inside our compound,” said Kamona, 24, who gave only one name.

“We have children, but they don’t care.”

Industry representatives said workers from at least 529 factories in Dhaka and its surrounding industrial areas, including Savar, Ashulia, Jirani and Gazipur, had left their workplaces on Sunday.

item.title: Wage board set as unrest shuts Bangladesh garment factories
item.description:
DHAKA: Bangladesh said on Sunday it had set up a wage board to review garment workers’ pay and urged employees to return to work as violent protests forced the closure of more than 500 factories, with police firing tear gas and water cannon at demonstrators.

The dispute has raised concerns about widespread disruption to an industry that employs about four million workers, generates more than 80pc of Bangladesh’s export earnings and supplies clothing to many leading Western brands.

The workers in the South Asian nation are demanding a minimum monthly wage of 30,000 taka ($245), more than double the current 12,500 taka, saying rising costs of food, housing, transport and healthcare have sharply eroded their purchasing power.

“The cost of living has increased far beyond our incomes,” worker Mahin Hossain said. “After paying rent, there is very little left for food, our children’s education and other essential expenses. Many are finding it almost impossible to support their families.”

Police use tear gas

Despite the announcement of the wage board, thousands of garment workers staged demonstrations on Sunday, blocking roads in Dhaka and Gazipur, outside the capital, and disrupting transport across key industrial areas.

Police used tear gas and water cannon to disperse protesters after demonstrators threw bricks at officers, and a police vehicle and a police box were set on fire in separate incidents. Authorities deployed Border Guard Bangladesh personnel to maintain order.

The latest unrest follows demonstrations in Ashulia, a major garment manufacturing hub on the outskirts of Dhaka, where dozens of factories suspended operations on Saturday after workers staged protests demanding higher pay.

In all, the unrest has forced 529 garment factories to shut down and left 987,190 workers out of work across the country’s main industrial hubs, according to the Bangladesh Garment Manufacturers and Exporters Association.

Labour and Employment Minister Ariful Haque Choudhury said the wage board was formed after discussions with workers’ representatives and industry leaders, and urged workers to resume work.

The six-member wage board comprises two representatives each from workers and employers, along with a government representative and a neutral member. The body has been tasked with reviewing wages in the garment sector and recommending revised pay rates.

Delayed shipments

Choudhury warned that prolonged disruptions could delay export shipments and payments from international buyers, creating further difficulties for manufacturers and workers alike. Bangladesh’s ready-made garment industry, the world’s largest after China, contributes about 10pc of gross domestic product and is the backbone of the economy.

Manufacturers, however, say the sector is facing mounting challenges, including rising production costs, periodic gas and electricity shortages, and uncertainty in energy markets linked to tensions in the Middle East.

Govt employees receive salaries under new pay structure after 11 years
item.description:
Government officials and employees received their salaries under the new pay structure on Sunday, along with arrears of increased salaries for July, August and September.
Many government employees received SMS notifications on their mobile phones after 10am, confirming the payment of their October salaries and the additional amounts due for the previous three months.
According to officials at the Finance Division of the Ministry of Finance, nearly all of the country's 1.4 million government employees, 800,000 pensioners and 600,000 MPO-listed teachers received the increased payments.
However, there were also employees who could not receive their revised salaries as their pay fixation process remained incomplete.
Several government officials said they received notifications confirming the payment under the revised pay structure from around 10am. They expect the remaining employees to receive their payments within the next two to three days after completing the pay fixation process.
The government issued a gazette notification announcing the new National Pay Scale on September 17, retaining the existing 20 grades of government employees while deciding to increase basic salaries by up to 142%.
Under the revised structure, basic salaries for employees in grades one to 11 increased by 100%, while those in grades 12 to 20 received increases ranging from 115 to 142%.
The new pay structure came into effect on July 1, 2026, with implementation scheduled in phases rather than through a single adjustment.
According to the notification, from July 1 to December 31, 2026, officials in grade nine and above will receive 40 percent of the increased basic salary while employees in grades 10 to 20 will receive 50% of the increase.
The additional amount has been calculated against the salaries drawn or due on June 30, 2026.
From January 1 to June 30, 2027, employees will receive 75 percent of the increased basic salary. The government will implement 100 percent of the revised pay scale, including annual increments, from July 1, 2027.
All other allowances will continue at the rates applicable on June 30, 2026, until December 31, 2027. The revised allowance rates announced in the gazette will take effect from January 1, 2028.
The previous National Pay Scale came into effect in 2015, making the latest revision the first major restructuring of government salaries in 11 years.
Under the 2015 pay scale, basic salaries increased by 95% at the highest grade and 101% at the lowest grade.

item.title: What the LDC extension means for Bangladeshi industries
item.description:
The United Nations General Assembly's decision to extend Bangladesh’s Least Developed Country (LDC) graduation timeline to November 2029 offers a crucial breathing space for an economy navigating global supply chain disruptions and political transition.
By deferring the immediate withdrawal of duty-free, quota-free (DFQF) market access, the decision protects Bangladeshi merchandise exports from an average tariff burden of 12.50% across 38 destination countries.
Yet, while industrial leaders breathe a sigh of relief, economic experts warn against treating this deferment as a license for delay.
The three-year grace period must not become a comfortable plateau, but rather an active launching pad for deep structural transformation, capacity building, and industrial modernization.
For Bangladesh’s flagship export sector—the readymade garment (RMG) industry—the deferment provides immediate tariff security in key markets across the European Union, United Kingdom, and regional trading blocs.
It buys vital time to negotiate bilateral trade agreements and preferential trade frameworks that can replace LDC-specific privileges after 2029.
Similarly, the local pharmaceutical sector gains temporary protection under the World Trade Organization’s TRIPS flexibilities.
This preserves local manufacturing rights for generic drugs and patented formulations without domestic price spikes on essential medicines like insulin and anti-retroviral treatments.
For non-exporting local industries—ranging from light engineering and consumer electronics to agriculture-linked processing—the temporary continuation of protective tariffs buys time to build scale and improve cost efficiency.
However, reliance on state support will become increasingly unsustainable as global trade rules require progressive tariff rationalization.
Capacity building imperative
The core challenge facing Bangladeshi industries over the next six years is no longer just tariff preferences—it is international competitiveness.
Modern trade buyers and import markets prioritize factory efficiency, regulatory compliance, and environmental standards over artificially subsidized prices.

Converting time into action
The extended timeline till November 2029 effectively provides Bangladesh with a total six-year buffer when factoring in post-graduation transition support.
However, past experience shows that long timelines without accountability often breed reform inertia.
To prevent history from repeating itself, the government must convert its Smooth Transition Strategy (STS) into a binding, time-bound policy roadmap.
Clear benchmarks, institutional accountability, and quarterly progress tracking will be necessary to ensure policy implementation keeps pace with international demands.
For private enterprises, the message is equally clear: government subsidies and trade protections will eventually end.
The true measure of success for this three-year extension will be determined not by the tariffs avoided today, but by the productivity, sustainability, and technological capabilities built for tomorrow.

item.title: Pakistani High Commissioner meets Speaker Hafiz Uddin Ahmad
item.description:
Pakistani High Commissioner to Bangladesh Imran Haider paid a courtesy call on Speaker Hafiz Uddin Ahmad at the latter’s office in the city on Sunday.
During the meeting at the National Parliament, the speaker thanked the government of Pakistan for supporting Barrister Jahrat Adib Chowdhury, chairman of the Parliamentary Standing Committee on Ministry of Foreign Affairs of the Bangladesh Parliament, as a member of the Inter-Parliamentary Union (IPU) Executive Committee at the 153rd IPU Assembly held in Tanzania.
Both sides emphasized the importance of forming the parliamentary friendship group between Bangladesh and Pakistan and exchanging visits by parliamentary delegations.
They also exchanged views on providing training to officials and employees of the Bangladesh Parliament Secretariat at Pakistan's legislature, Majlis-e-Shoora.
The speaker invited the Pakistani high commissioner to observe the upcoming session of the Bangladesh Parliament, which will begin on November 09.
Speaker Hafiz Uddin Ahmad, Bir Bikram, will visit Pakistan on November 23 at the invitation of the Speaker of Pakistan Parliament, according to a press release.
Representatives of the Pakistan High Commission, the Secretary of the Bangladesh Parliament Secretariat and other senior officials concerned were present at the meeting.

item.title: PM orders steps to protect garment workers’ interests, keep production uninterrupted
item.description:
Prime Minister Tarique Rahman on Sunday directed the authorities concerned to protect garment workers’ interests and ensure uninterrupted production and export activities in the apparel sector.
Home Minister Salahuddin Ahmed came up with the prime minister’s instructions while talking to reporters after a meeting on the prevailing situation in the garment sector at the Secretariat at night.
At the same time, he warned that those involved in violence, sabotage and attempts to create disorder in the name of workers’ movement will be dealt with strictly.
“The prime minister has given advice and directives to ensure that garment workers’ interests are protected, their living standards improve, and production and development in Bangladesh are not disrupted, while exports increase. He has asked us to take steps keeping all these issues in consideration,” he said.
Salahuddin said the law enforcement agencies have been asked to take strict action against those who are involved in violence or attempting to create disorder and instability.
“We have asked the law enforcement agencies to deal firmly with those who are involved in violence, behaving recklessly or trying to create unnecessary disorder and instability,” he said.
The minister alleged that masked individuals infiltrated different levels of the incidents during the day and that some quarters from across the border were instigating innocent garment workers to create instability and disrupt the country's export trade and apparel production.
“Analysing the information available to the government, we have found that some people from across the border are instigating innocent garment workers to create instability in the country, disrupt export trade and hamper production in the garment industry,” he said.
The government will deal strictly with such activities, Salahuddin said, adding that those involved in violent acts are being brought under the law.
“Police and other law enforcement agencies will take strict action against any attempt at sabotage or creating disorder,” he added.
The minister said the government formed a wage board to revise the minimum wages of garment workers, stressing that there is no need for violent demonstrations as the issue can be resolved through discussions.
He said the law provides for the formation of a wage board every three years to review workers’ minimum wages. “Although there is time until December to form the board, the government has taken the initiative earlier through discussions with representatives of employers and workers.”
The employers had submitted the names of their representatives, but there was a delay in receiving nominations from workers’ organisations, Salahuddin said, adding that after receiving the worker representatives’ names on Saturday night, the government formed the board and issued a notification on Sunday morning.
The representatives of employers and workers on the board will discuss and recommend minimum wages, taking into account workers’ living standards, their ability to maintain a decent family life and their financial capacity, he said.
The minister said the government is sincere about protecting workers’ interests and improving their living standards.
He, however, alleged that violence took place in the name of the workers’ movement, including setting fire to police vehicles, attacks at different places, vandalism of vehicles and arson at factories. “There was no need for such violence when the issue of wages could be discussed and resolved through dialogue,” he said.
Salahuddin said the prime minister instructed the authorities concerned to ensure workers’ welfare and improve their living standards.
Tarique Rahman also advised the wage board and asked the Ministry of Labour and Employment to take necessary steps to protect workers’ interests, he said.
The government wants peace, discipline, development and progress, the minister said, adding that its goal is to expand the garment industry, increase export earnings and create more employment opportunities for workers.
He also recalled the contribution of Shaheed President Ziaur Rahman to the development of Bangladesh’s garment industry, saying the government wants the sector to grow further, exports to expand and employment opportunities to increase.
Asked whether factories closed amid the unrest will reopen on Monday, Salahuddin said garment factory owners have been urged to keep production running.
“If any factory has been closed for some reason, the closure should be temporary. Owners and workers should maintain normal production through mutual discussions and understanding,” he said.
The minister stressed that production and supply of goods for export must not be disrupted under any circumstances.
Asked when the wage board will hold its first meeting, he advised reporters to contact the board chairman for details.
The meeting began at 6pm at the Cabinet Division conference room of the Secretariat to review the situation surrounding the garment workers’ movement and clashes with police at different places.
Those present included Prime Minister’s Political Adviser Nazrul Islam Khan, Home Minister Salahuddin Ahmed, Labour and Employment Minister Ariful Haque Choudhury, State Minister for Local Government, Rural Development and Co-operatives Mir Shahe Alam, Prime Minister’s Adviser Mahdi Amin and Jatiyatabadi Sramik Dal Chief Coordinator Shamsur Rahman Shimul Biswas, MP.

This statement was made by the Home Minister in response to a question at a press conference after a meeting with the leaders of BGMEA and BKMEA, organisations of garment industry owners, at the Secretariat on Monday morning.

Informing that cooperation from garment factory owners was sought during the meeting, the Home Minister said some industrialists deliberately closed factories. The leaders of the owners' organisations have been asked to provide a list of them. At the same time, a list of worker leaders and organisations involved in creating unrest has been sought.

1 detained over ‘Facebook post’ about setting fire to police vehicle in Mirpur

The Home Minister mentioned that arrangements have been made for 24-hour surveillance to monitor the situation in the garment industry.

He said specific persons have been appointed for communication from the Ministry of Home Affairs and the Police Department. There will also be designated persons for communication from the owners' organisations.

For this, instructions have been given to establish a control room at the police headquarters. The situation will be monitored from there through security apps.

The Home Minister said, "We do not want any factory to close, not even for a moment."

The Minister stated that those who are engaged in anti-labour activities in the guise of labour movements and are trying to create instability in the country will be dealt with strictly.

He said legal action will be taken in this regard. No actual workers are involved in this unrest.

For the past few days, garment factory workers have been protesting demanding a minimum wage of Tk 30,000. To resolve the ongoing crisis, the Home Minister held a meeting with the leaders of BGMEA and BKMEA at the conference room of the Ministry of Home Affairs on Monday morning.

Speaking at a press conference after the meeting, the Home Minister alleged that for some time now, some supporters of fallen tyrannical fascism are using innocent workers to create unrest. Those who are trying to create unrest by blocking roads and highways and setting fires have been identified.

Garment workers try to take to the streets through Mirpur alleys, police disperse them

The Home Minister further said, "We would like to categorically state very sternly that those who are involved in anti-law enforcement activities under the guise of a labour movement, and those who are engaging in conspiracy to create instability in the country by creating unrest, will be sternly suppressed. Legal measures will be taken."

The Minister said that a few such individuals have been brought under the law today. He said video footage and some evidence of their activities have been collected. There are audios, videos, and visual video clips of various violent incidents.

The Minister said that the government has already formed a wage board. The first meeting of the board may be held today, he said. Even if not today, they will sit down within a very short time, and after discussion, the minimum wage will be determined and announced as soon as possible, he said.

Dhaka-Tangail highway blocked again by garment workers, BGB deployed

The Home Minister further said that the demand for setting up a Minimum Wage Board for workers every three years is something the government initiated weeks ago. The name of the representative from the owners' side was also provided. But the worker organisations took a few days to provide names. They provided the name of their representative the night before last. The Wage Board has been formed through a proper process by notification with names from both the worker and owner sides.

Meeting with labour union leaders in the afternoon

The Home Minister said that the government will meet with representatives of labour unions at around 3 PM today. The views and suggestions of the labour leaders will be heard there. Future steps will be taken based on their opinions.

Regarding the return of former Prime Minister Sheikh Hasina to the country in the coming December, he said, "Fascist forces and fugitive leaders who want to return should do so quickly. Why should it take until December? We want to ensure justice by bringing them under the law swiftly."

Expatriate Welfare Minister Ariful Haque Chowdhury, Prime Minister's Advisor Mahadi Amin, labour leader, and Member of Parliament Shimul Biswas were present at the press conference.

item.title: Cyclone ‘Murasu’ likely to cross south Andhra Pradesh coast by early 3 Nov: IMD
item.description:
ANI_20261101559

Cyclonic Storm Murasu intensified into a severe cyclonic storm over the west-central and adjoining southwest Bay of Bengal and is likely to cross the south Andhra Pradesh coast between midnight on 2 November and the early hours of 3 November, the India Meteorological Department (IMD) said.

In its latest bulletin, the IMD said the system moved nearly northwestwards at a speed of 20 kmph during the past six hours and lay centred over the same region at 2:30 am IST on 2 November.

The severe cyclonic storm was centred near latitude 13.6°N and longitude 82.5°E, about 260 km east-northeast of Chennai, 290 km east-southeast of Nellore, 320 km south-southeast of Machilipatnam, 310 km east-southeast of Kavali, 330 km southeast of Ongole and 470 km south of Visakhapatnam.

The weather agency said the storm is very likely to continue moving northwestwards and cross the south Andhra Pradesh coast as a severe cyclonic storm, with a sustained wind speed of 100–110 kmph and gusts reaching 120 kmph.

The landfall is likely between Nellore and Narsapur, close to Ongole, between 11:30 pm IST on 2 and 4 November am IST on 3 November, the IMD said.

Meanwhile, the Rayagada district administration has stepped up its preparedness for the possible impact of Cyclone Murasu, deploying all 11 fire station teams and heavy machinery at strategic locations for emergency response, Additional District Magistrate (General) Ravindranath Kahanra said.

The administration held a virtual emergency review meeting on Sunday under the chairmanship of the District Collector to assess preparedness for the possible cyclone and heavy rainfall.

The meeting reviewed early warning systems, emergency services, rescue and relief operations, shelter arrangements and the availability of essential equipment.

Speaking about the preparedness measures, Kahanra said, “In preparation for Cyclone Murasu, the Rayagada District Collector held a virtual emergency meeting to discuss safety measures and readiness. Key topics included the district's preparedness, early warning systems, emergency services, and shelter preparations.”

He said that, based on reports from the India Meteorological Department (IMD) and the Special Relief Commissioner (SRC), the district was under a yellow warning until 2 November, followed by an orange warning for 3 and 4 November.

The administration has deployed all 11 fire station teams and positioned JCBs, excavators and Hydra cranes at Gumma Ghati and Mukundpur Ghati for immediate clearance of National Highway 326 in case of road blockages.

Kahanra said, “The administration has deployed fire station teams and machinery for road clearance, while BDOs, Tahsildars and concerned officials have been instructed to remain present with all equipment and machinery to prepare for any type of eventuality.”

item.title: Trial begins in New York for 2 former Cleveland Guardians pitchers facing fraud charges
item.description:
Former Cleveland Guardians pitchers Emmanuel Clase and Luis Ortiz go to trial Monday on charges that they accepted bribes as they colluded with gamblers who made hundreds of thousands of dollars betting correctly on individual pitches.

Their careers and possibly their freedom are at stake in the jury trial expected to unfold over the next month in Brooklyn federal court. Several professional baseball players, including catchers and baseball executives, are among witnesses expected to testify.

Clase, the Guardians’ former closer, and Ortiz, a starter, have pleaded not guilty to conspiracy charges and are on nondisciplinary leave from the club without pay while their fate is determined.

According to an indictment, the pitchers accepted several thousand dollars in payoffs to help two gamblers from their native Dominican Republic win at least $460,000 on in-game prop bets on the speed and outcome of certain pitches.

Prosecutors allege that Clase began providing the bettors with information about his pitches in 2023 and recruited Ortiz into the scheme in 2025. Lawyers for Ortiz unsuccessfully sought to have Ortiz tried separately from Clase.

Judge Kiyo A. Matsumoto said at a conference Friday that she hopes to complete jury selection quickly enough that lawyers can deliver relatively short opening statements in the afternoon.

Clase, 28, is a three-time All-Star and two-time American League Reliever of the Year who had completed his fourth season of a $20 million, five-year contract when charges against the pitchers were revealed in November 2025.

Ortiz, 27, had earned $782,600 as a starting pitcher for the Guardians during the 2025 season.

The pitchers have been charged with wire fraud conspiracy, honest services wire fraud conspiracy, money laundering conspiracy and conspiracy to influence sporting contests by bribery.

Defense lawyers are expected to argue that the pitchers did not collude with gamblers and instead were varying the placement of pitches strategically to fool batters.

On Friday, the judge ruled that prosecutors cannot show the jury proof that Clase owed $500,000 in U.S. taxes because they had only provided the evidence to defense lawyers several days earlier and long after a deadline had passed to turn over evidence to their adversaries.

A prosecutor had argued that the government wanted to put the evidence in the trial to offset any claim by Clase’s lawyers that he had no incentive to collude with gamblers because he had several million dollars in financial accounts in the Dominican Republic.

Major League Baseball and the Guardians have both said they’ve fully cooperated with authorities. MLB has said it contacted federal law enforcement when it began investigating unusual betting activity.

—Associated Press

Will ‘strategic stability’ with China go out the window if Trump loses the midterms?
Britain's elites are in hysterics over looming 'war' with Russia
item.description:
British Defense Secretary Wes Streeting recently said the U.K. has 1000 days to be “ready with our allies to fight and win.” The enemy is obvious: Russia. The catch: London doesn’t have the cash to fight, and ordinary folk aren’t interested.

This latest reminder that war with our Slavic foes is imminent is vague and unspecified, and frankly tedious. As the Wall Street Journal pointed out nearly a year ago, “rarely a week goes by now without a European government, military or security chief making a grim speech warning the public that they are headed toward a potential war with Russia.”

Streeting is simply the latest to join the chorus. Earlier in October, he advised British people to stock up on tinned food and bottled water in case of an emergency, a suggestion he has since repeated.

Yet a gap is growing between this war readiness rhetoric and the reality of public finances in Britain. It is evident that the government has little fiscal headroom to increase defense spending rapidly to the NATO target of 3.5% of GDP by 2035. In his annual budget statement last week, Chancellor (and former Defense Secretary) John Healy said the 3% target would be reached “in the next Parliament,” which could be as late as 2034. Current spending plans suggest U.K. defense won’t go beyond 2.7% this decade.

We can’t afford to expand our army which, at 73,500 troops, is already at its smallest since 1823, according to MoD data. There are more than 700,000 Russian troops in Ukraine alone. When discussions kicked off in March 2025 about a “coalition of the willing” peacekeeping force for Ukraine, the U.K. armed forces were considered “too stretched” to contribute without cutting back operations elsewhere. A British MP and member of the U.K. parliamentary defense select committee told me we would struggle to put 10,000 troops on the field.

Nevertheless, a concerted campaign appears underway to soften Brits up for the fight. This past weekend, the Spectator put out a piece calling for the reintroduction of mandatory National Service for 18-year-olds. “What we need is a resilient, hardened and capable population, ready for the tough times ahead,” wrote Ted Jeffery. “Not a country with 10 million working-age people on benefits.”

No one talks about how to pay for schemes like this, except, one assumes, to cut back on benefits. Herein lies the guns or butter faultline in British political discussion, which you can also witness in Germany and in France. The state should cut back on public services such as welfare and instead spend money on defense and war readiness.

The protests and riots that have rocked France are not driven by concerns about the risk of war, but rather about the dilapidation of the school system. This past weekend has also seen riots across Germany about the cost of living. Former German Foreign Minister Annalena Baerbock’s suggestion that she would back Ukraine “no matter what voters think” helps explain why increasing numbers of Germans are turning to parties such as Alternative für Deutschland (AfD).

Foreign policy starts and ends at home. Ordinary folk spend little time thinking about foreign policy and assume that their governments will focus on domestic concerns. That gives elected leaders considerable scope to cut a dash on the world stage in the face of public indifference. However, it does not offer carte blanche to put foreign issues first.

In Britain, the public doesn’t appear remotely interested in fighting a foreign war. A recent poll by Ipsos found that 48% of Britons would not agree to fight “under any circumstances” while only 36% might be willing.

Indeed, the most interesting observation was that the age group most willing was the over 55s. This cohort might get its chance as last week the government announced it had updated its policies determining that reservists up to 65 years of age could be reactivated "to strengthen UK readiness as global threats continue to grow."

The British Foreign Policy Group’s 2026 Survey also indicated that 52% of Britons would be unwilling, and 58% unable, to fight, with a similar tilt towards the older generation.

The government has made some effort to persuade its citizens to change their minds. In late October, the Head of the Army, Sir Roland Walker, warned that “our citizens have got to consent to sacrifices to prioritize defense and security.” This follows on from the highly publicized remarks on GB News that pro-Russian (read pro-peace) voices should be locked up and conscription should be introduced.

The latter was pure bloviation. The former, an incitement by a serving military officer to put conscription into practice. This was leapt upon by historian Peter Hitchens, who wrote that it was not for serving military officers “to put the case for sacrifices by the voting public. Nor was it for him to tell politicians to explain this to the public.” I heartily agree.

British ministers and pundits never explain where we might meet the Russians in battle after we’ve been press-ganged and put into uniforms. Anyone who believes they are going to romp all the way across Europe and cross the channel to meet us here must be a fantasist. That means we either go into Ukraine, which we have steadfastly avoided doing since 2014, or we send our troops to a NATO country that is attacked, despite the lack of evidence that Russia has any intention of launching such an endeavor.

A more credible, less expensive and less dangerous approach would be to engage in diplomacy to put an end to conflict, rather than allowing it to fester and worsen. With a government too poor to grow the army and with a population unwilling to fight, Britain nevertheless clings to its refusal to talk and engage in diplomacy. At the recent G20 Foreign Ministers’ meeting in Atlanta, Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband, beside a grinning Foreign Minister Radek Sikorski of Poland, used the plenary to lambast Russian Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov and declare “you are not winning the war”.

A planned family photo, where the ministers all stand together, was canceled because the Brits and Europeans didn’t want to be in shot with Lavrov. Further proof, sadly, that statecraft in Britain and Europe today resembles a bunch of 10-year-olds squabbling in the schoolyard.

item.title: Australia's Glenn Maxwell calls time on international career
item.description:
Explosive batsman Glenn Maxwell announced his international retirement Tuesday after being overlooked for Australia’s upcoming Twenty20 series against England.

The mercurial 38-year-old, who had not played a Test since 2017, called time on his one-day career last year but kept the door open for T20s.

He has not been picked since the World Cup in Sri Lanka in February, with selectors bypassing him for a series against Bangladesh in June.

Maxwell was again overlooked for the squad named Monday to play England in November, with a host of younger players instead preferred.

“A little bit sad and a little bit inevitable too, but I’m announcing my retirement from international cricket,” Maxwell said on the Final Word podcast.

“We probably had numerous discussions before and after the T20 World Cup,” he added of talks with selectors. “And it was pretty open-ended.

“There wasn’t any pressure from (Australia team management), and we decided to sort of leave the door open.

“There was a couple of series that were coming up (in which) they were going to look to the future, and we saw that in Bangladesh with guys getting their opportunity and performing really well.

“There was a small hope or discussion that I might have been able to potentially get a send-off game at the Melbourne Cricket Ground (against England).

“But I can completely understand the direction they’re going with this squad.” Maxwell played 130 T20 internationals, blasting 2,897 runs with a strike rate of 154.42, leaving as Australia’s third-highest run-scorer after David Warner and Aaron Finch.

While he only played seven Tests, he featured in 149 ODIs, crunching 3,990 runs.

Maxwell also called time on his first-class career with Victoria, but will continue with the Melbourne Renegades in the Big Bash League.

“I’m grateful for the time I was able to play for my country,” he said.

“If you had offered me that career when I first walked into the Victoria change rooms in 2009-ish, I would have bitten your hand off.”

item.title: Maaz Sadaqat, Hasan Nawaz named in Pakistan Shaheens squad for Rising Stars Asia Cup
item.description:
Maaz Sadaqat and Hasan Nawaz have been included in the 15-member Pakistan Shaheens squad for the ACC Men’s Asia Cup Rising Stars 2026, with Abdul Samad appointed captain for the 50-over tournament to be held in Qatar from Nov 19 to 29.

The Pakistan Cricket Board announced the squad on Tuesday, with the Shaheens set to defend the title they won in the previous 50-over edition in 2023. Pakistan are also the defending champions of the T20 version of the competition, having beaten Bangladesh A in a final decided by a Super Over.

The eight-team tournament will feature two groups of four sides. Pakistan have been placed in Group ‘B’ alongside India A, Nepal and the United Arab Emirates, while Group ‘A’ comprises Afghanistan A, Bangladesh A, Hong Kong China and Sri Lanka A.

The Shaheens will open their campaign against the UAE on Nov 20, before taking on India A two days later and Nepal on Nov 24. Their first match will be played at the University of Doha Science and Technology ground, with the remaining group fixtures scheduled at the West End Park International Cricket Stadium.

All three group matches are day-night fixtures except the opening game, which will be played during the day. The semi-finals are scheduled for Nov 26 and 27, with the final to be held on Nov 29.

Samad will lead a batting group that includes Maaz, Hasan, Haider Ali, Shahzaib Khan, Farhan Yousuf and Shamyl Hussain. Rohail Nazir has been named as the designated wicket-keeper.

The squad also includes three spin options in left-arm spin all-rounder Danish Aziz, leg-spinner Saad Masood and Sufyan Moqim. The pace attack will be led by Mohammad Hasnain and also features Ahmed Daniyal, Akif Javed and Muhammad Imran Randhawa.

Ahmed Daniyal was part of the Shaheens side that won the previous T20 edition, playing a key role as the team clinched the title against Bangladesh A in a Super Over.

Pakistan won the last 50-over edition in Sri Lanka in 2023, beating India A by 128 runs in the final. They were runners-up in the opening two editions in 2013 and 2017 before winning the competition in 2019.

The Shaheens will be aiming to retain their title against a field that includes several of the region’s emerging sides, with a meeting against India A among the key fixtures in the group stage.

item.title: Seven migrants drown off Canary Islands
item.description:
MADRID: At least seven migrants died off Spain’s Canary Islands while more than 380 people were rescued on Monday, the country’s maritime rescue services said.

Two deceased people were found aboard a migrant boat when the coast guard rescued 132 people on Monday, 150 km off Lanzarote. During the same journey, five other migrants had died and been thrown into the sea, authorities added.

Another 250 migrants were rescued by coast guard boats off Lanzarote and the Canary Island of El Hierro earlier on Monday, authorities said. On Sunday, 107 migrants were rescued off El Hierro, according to authorities.

“The worst forecasts are coming true. The Atlantic route is once again claiming lives, this time off the coast of Lanzarote. Behind each one is a life, a story, and a family,” Canary Islands President Fernando Clavijo said in a message on X.

The Atlantic route from West Africa to the Canary Islands is one of the world’s deadliest migration crossings. Thousands of migrants attempt the journey each year in overcrowded boats, seeking to reach Spanish territory despite rough seas, strong currents and long distances.

Arrivals tend to pick up in the autumn months, when sea conditions along the route are generally calmer and more favourable for crossings.

Migrant arrivals have declined so far this year compared with the same period in 2025, but crossings increased sharply in October, putting additional pressure on reception and emergency services on some of the Canary Islands, particularly the smaller and less densely populated ones.

Migrant arrivals in the archipelago have fallen 18pc year on year to 11,527 people, according to the office of the Spanish government’s representative in the Canary Islands.

Asylum seekers deported

Spain has returned to Morocco more than a dozen sub-Saharan African and Asian migrants who reached the Spanish enclave of Ceuta and were turned down for asylum, the first deportation of its kind from the enclave since a mass border crossing in July.

The Interior Ministry said the group had been sent back to Morocco after it agreed to receive them and they remained on Moroccan territory at present. It declined to give numbers or nationalities but migrant and rights charities operating in Ceuta said 16 people from Senegal, Nigeria, Yemen, Cameroon and Bangladesh were deported.

The NGOs claim such returns fail to take into account the risks associated with Morocco’s treatment of migrants from other countries and fly in the face of the values espoused by Spain’s leftist government.

Virginia Alvarez, an Amnesty International researcher, said Spain’s posture was hypocritical. “Spain, despite its [progressive] speeches in Europe, is not ensuring that human rights guarantees are met for people who cross its borders in Ceuta and Melilla,” she said. “Morocco does not respect many human rights.”

Published in Dawn, November 3rd, 2026

Cabinet approves 29 public holidays for 2027
item.description:
The cabinet has approved 29 public holidays for 2027, including 15 general holidays and 14 holidays declared by executive order, with 22 effective holidays after excluding those coinciding with weekly weekends.
The decision was taken at the 26th cabinet meeting, held at the secretariat on Monday. Following the meeting, Cabinet Secretary Nasimul Gani briefed journalists at the conference room of the Department of Information.
Nasimul Gani said the approved holiday list includes 15 general holidays for national days and various religious festivals. Of these, 4 days will coincide with weekly holidays, comprising 2 Fridays and 2 Saturdays.
Another 14 holidays will be declared by executive order for the Bengali New Year and various religious festivals. Of these, 3 days will coincide with weekly holidays, including 1 Friday and 2 Saturdays.
As a result, 7 of the 29 holidays will overlap with weekly holidays, leaving 22 effective public holidays in 2027.
According to the approved list, employees of the Republic will be allowed up to 3 optional holidays annually for various religious festivals.
Government employees from small ethnic groups working in the Chittagong Hill Tracts and other parts of the country will also be entitled to 2 optional holidays to celebrate their main social festival, Boisabi, or similar festivals.

item.title: E-immigration launched at Shahjalal airport arrival counters, easing passenger hassle
item.description:
An automated border control system, or e-gate, has been introduced at the arrival counters of Hazrat Shahjalal International Airport in Dhaka, allowing e-passport holders to complete immigration in just 18 to 20 seconds and avoid long queues.
The introduction of e-gates at the arrivals section has eased passenger hassle and significantly reduced the time required for immigration, officials said.
Speaking to Dhaka Tribune on Monday afternoon, Department of Immigration and Passports (DIP) Director General Major General Md Alimul Amin said e-gates had been introduced at the airport’s arrival counters and passengers could now complete immigration within a very short time.
“We also want to introduce e-gate services at departures. We are working on it,” he said.
However, he said the departure service was not yet technically ready. Although passengers’ passports can be scanned at the departure e-gates, the system cannot currently complete the required stamping process, leaving the service suspended.
During a visit to the airport, a Dhaka Tribune correspondent found that passengers still have to collect their arrival stickers manually from a police booth after completing e-immigration.
Officials said the process would be simplified once the third terminal becomes operational, and passengers would no longer have to visit the police booth separately to collect their arrival stickers.
Airport immigration officials said Bangladesh faces several technical and operational challenges in fully digitising immigration services, including e-gates and e-visa verification.
These challenges include an insufficient number of e-gates and barcode and biometric reader devices, frequent server downtime and delays in IT systems.
There is also no real-time integration among the databases of the National Identity Card (NID) system, the Department of Immigration and Passports (DIP) and the Bureau of Manpower, Employment and Training (BMET).
As a result, even minor discrepancies in passengers’ names or dates of birth can prevent e-gates from automatically identifying them.
Technical problems with facial-recognition cameras and fingerprint-matching systems can also cause the gates to reject legitimate passengers. In addition, some immigration officials lack the technical expertise needed to operate digital systems and verify e-visas.
Major General Alimul Amin said several technical, institutional and practical challenges remain in converting departure immigration into a fully digital system.
“That is why the service is currently suspended. But we are working to simplify this service, as well as passport-related services, as soon as possible,” he said.
Passengers said the introduction of e-gates at arrivals had reduced both waiting time and hassle, allowing them to complete immigration automatically within 18 to 20 seconds.
Liton Kabir, who recently returned from Thailand, told Dhaka Tribune: “The e-passport was once a dream for the people of Bangladesh. The e-gate was introduced alongside it. Although the service was closed for various reasons, I feel relieved now that it has reopened. If it is introduced at departures soon, travelling will become even easier.”
Rajib Ahmed, who recently returned from Turkey, said the service had made the arrival process much easier.
“This was our first family tour. With an e-passport, you can clear immigration in about 18 seconds. It would have been great to have the facility at departures too, as it would save a lot of time. The government should pay attention to this,” he said.
An immigration official said passengers using e-gates at departures still have to return to the immigration desk for visa verification and other checks, meaning the process takes almost as long as before.
“This makes passengers angry. Data from the e-gates also often fails to reach the immigration software. That is why the departure e-gates have remained closed,” he said.
He added that while e-gates are currently closed for departing passengers at Shahjalal Airport, they are operational for arriving passengers.
Bangladesh introduced e-passports in February 2020, becoming the first country in South Asia to do so. E-gates were subsequently installed at Hazrat Shahjalal International Airport to facilitate faster and more efficient immigration processing.
However, technical problems and the continued need for manual visa verification and other checks created complications. As a result, passengers still had to visit immigration desks even after using the e-gates, prompting authorities to suspend their operation.
Several members of the Immigration Police's Special Branch, speaking on condition of anonymity, said around 40% of passengers using the airport each day hold e-passports.
They said the e-gates can automatically verify passport and passenger information but cannot independently verify visas.
The system also lacks provisions to automatically store information on passengers’ destinations or flights.
Consequently, visa verification continues to be conducted manually, even when passengers use the e-gates. This contributes to long queues at departure immigration, particularly when several flights arrive or depart around the same time.
Hazrat Shahjalal International Airport Executive Director Group Captain SM Ragib Samad told Dhaka Tribune that the e-gates can currently verify only passport information and cannot verify visas and other details.
“That is why the e-gates have been kept closed at departures. But we hope the service will start soon,” he said.
The government has taken an initiative to modernise Bangladesh's immigration system by integrating the existing Immigration Management System (IMS) with new technologies.
The Ministry of Home Affairs has formed a 10-member committee to review fee-setting, payment collection and settlement procedures under the system and develop an appropriate financial model.
The notice was issued on October 19 by the Departure-4 branch of the ministry's Security Services Division and published on October 25.
According to the notice, the government plans to integrate the Advance Passenger Information System (APIS), Passenger Name Record (PNR), e-Visa and Electronic Travel Authorisation (ETA) systems, as well as a sovereign data analytics platform, with the existing IMS.
The government is also considering appointing a third party to modernise the relevant infrastructure and implement the programme. As part of the initiative, the committee will review immigration facilitation charges, revenue collection and remittance procedures, and payment mechanisms. It will also prepare proposals on appropriate fees and a suitable financial model.
The committee is headed by the Joint Secretary of the Planning-1 wing of the Ministry of Home Affairs, while the Deputy Secretary of the Departure-4 branch will serve as its member-secretary.
Other members include the Joint Secretary of the Departure-1 wing of the Home Ministry and representatives from the Finance Division, National Board of Revenue (NBR), Civil Aviation Authority of Bangladesh (CAAB), Special Branch, Biman Bangladesh Airlines, Bangladesh Land Port Authority and the Department of Immigration and Passports.

item.title: Iran warns new war could last longer after Trump threatens strikes
item.description:
Iran warned on Sunday that any renewed war with the United States could last longer than the previous round of fighting, after President Donald Trump said he still had to “take care” of more targets.
Diplomatic efforts to end the Middle East war have been punctuated by repeated threats from the United States and Israel to resume bombardments as they hold crucial elections.
“A potential future war could last longer than previous conflict, and the American president would not be in a position to dictate the timing or the conditions of its conclusion,” said army spokesman Mohammad Akraminia, according to Iranian state television.
In the most intense phase of the war, which began on February 28 with US-Israeli strikes on Iran, Tehran retaliated with missile and drone attacks across the region. Iran-aligned armed groups joined the fighting in Lebanon and Yemen.
Akraminia’s remarks followed Trump’s suggestion that the United States could swiftly strike its remaining targets in Iran.
“We still have to take care of, I would say one or two sites, but we can do that in 10 minutes,” Trump told reporters.
“You probably could look at Pickaxe Mountain, and you have to take care of that. We can do that all very quickly,” he added, referring to a suspected underground nuclear complex.
Trump reiterated his threat on Sunday, telling a campaign rally in Iowa ahead of midterm elections, that he may have to give Tehran “the hammer” at some unspecified time.
The warning came after US media reported that Trump had held a call with Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu on Saturday over whether and when to ramp up combat operations against the Islamic Republic.
Axios quoted one US and one Israeli official saying the two leaders discussed the state of negotiations with Iran, with Netanyahu pressing the president to strike the country immediately after Tuesday’s US midterm elections and Trump eager to let negotiations play out.
The Israeli source described the call as “tough,” while the US source said it was “direct,” according to Axios.
Speaking to reporters on Sunday, Trump confirmed he had discussed Iran with Netanyahu, but would not elaborate.
Top military and political officials in Iran have warned against any new attack.
Revolutionary Guards spokesman Hossein Mohebbi on Sunday echoed a warning issued a day earlier in a written message by Iran’s new supreme leader, Ayatollah Mojtaba Khamenei.
“In a conflict with America, there are no geographical limitations; a vast theatre has been defined for inflicting damage upon the enemy,” Mohebbi said, according to state television.
Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi said: “We hope the other side will exercise rationality and choose diplomacy,” adding that Iran “remains prepared for both defense and diplomacy,” according to the official IRNA news agency.
The warnings came as Iran’s security chief Mohsen Rezaei disclosed on Saturday that he had received a letter from US Vice President JD Vance seeking to revive talks.
Rezaei noted what he described as a positive change in “tone” from the US side but said he had yet to respond.
He said Tehran had previously told Washington that unless its conditions were met, “neither would the Strait of Hormuz be reopened nor would there be any negotiations.”
Those conditions include unfreezing Iranian assets abroad, ending the months-long US naval blockade of Iranian ports, lifting longstanding sanctions and ending the war on all fronts.
Since the war began, Iran has claimed control over the Strait of Hormuz, a vital global energy conduit, and repeatedly targeted vessels attempting to cross without its authorization.
The United States has imposed a naval counter-blockade on Iranian ports.
Anwar Gargash, diplomatic adviser to the Emirati president, said on Sunday that the United Arab Emirates hoped the exchanges would yield a breakthrough, but was preparing for the worst.
“It is not the interest of the region to go through another round... But I think we’re also, as we’ve shown before, braced for the worst,” he told a conference in Manama.
In Tehran, some residents described a sense of helplessness as threats of renewed fighting mount.
“The news coming in is truly worrying. However... there is nothing I can actually do about it,” Mohadese, a 27-year-old health inspector, told AFP.
Others including 48-year-old vendor Ebrahim saw no reason to be concerned.
“We do not fear another war; we have been at war for 48 years now -- we are always at war,” he said in downtown Tehran.

item.title: Taliban government voices ‘serious concern’ over US Afghan deportation plans
item.description:
Afghanistan’s Taliban authorities voiced concern on Monday over reported plans by Washington to deport scores of Afghan immigrants to Pakistan with the aim of their eventual return to their home country.
More than 150 Afghans in the United States would be deported via Pakistan to Afghanistan, including relatives of those who assisted US forces before their 2021 withdrawal, according to US media reports and an advocacy group.
“The Islamic Emirate of Afghanistan expresses its serious concern over reports that the United States intends to deport some Afghan refugees to Pakistan who have not yet been able to obtain legal residency documents in that country,” foreign ministry spokesman Abdul Qahar Balkhi said in a statement.
Advocacy groups have warned that the removal of former allies and their families could endanger their lives.
After regaining power, Taliban authorities announced a general amnesty for Afghans who worked with Western-backed forces and governments and have repeated promises this year that their former foes could safely return home.
However, the United Nations has recorded reports of extrajudicial killings, detentions and abuses.
President Donald Trump’s administration last year issued travel bans for a number of countries, including Afghanistan, as part of a broad immigration crackdown.
His administration sought to end deportation protections for Afghans, some of whom were granted special immigrant visas following the 2021 takeover by Taliban authorities.
Among those expected to be deported are relatives of Afghans who assisted the US military in the country prior to the fall of Kabul, according to AfghanEvac, a group seeking to help former Afghan allies.
While the United States cannot arrange deportations directly to Afghanistan, anonymous US officials told The New York Times that Pakistan will oversee their expulsion to Afghanistan.
In recent years, Germany and Turkey have deported Afghan nationals directly to Afghanistan, despite concerns from human rights groups over the risks facing returnees.
Balkhi said Taliban authorities urged “the United States of America to adopt a responsible and measured approach in this regard and to take any decisions and measures regarding the fate of Afghan citizens with clear mutual understanding, necessary coordination, and consideration of the rights and legitimate demands of the individuals concerned.”
“The Afghan side is ready to interact in this regard in a practical and mutually understanding manner,” he added.
Pakistan’s government earlier this year ordered law enforcement nationwide to arrest Afghan citizens without visas as part of a years-long repatriation policy that has pushed back millions of Afghans who fled throughout decades of war.
Relations between Pakistan and Afghanistan have been fraught since the Taliban authorities took power and worsened after deadly border clashes last October that led to near-total closure of the border.

item.title: Democrats, Trump hold final rallies before midterm elections
item.description:
Democrats teed up final get-out-the-vote rallies Monday on the eve of midterm elections where they expect to win at least partial control of Congress and impose political constraints on President Donald Trump for the first time in two years.
Rallies -- including by star Democratic Senate candidates James Talarico in Texas and Adam Hamilton in Kansas -- were capping a campaign of breathtaking tension and bitterness.
For his closing argument, Trump chose a speech in Washington at the Lincoln Memorial Reflecting Pool -- a landmark that has become synonymous with the 80-year-old president’s obsessive, controversial drive to redevelop the US capital.
“We’re going to win,” he said on Sunday.
Polls, however, show that Democrats are near certain to take the majority from Republicans in the House of Representatives and have a real shot at winning the currently Republican Senate.
Even winning just the House would mean Democrats have voting power over the federal budget and would lead powerful committees able to investigate alleged corruption under Trump, the Epstein files and other explosive issues.
The loss of total Republican dominance would push Trump into unfamiliar and uncomfortable territory: a lame-duck period beset with high inflation at home, the sputtering war against Iran and hostile Democratic investigations into his activities in Washington.
But a decade into the Trump era, Democrats remain wary about predictions of victory.
“Nauseously optimistic,” Democratic Senator Raphael Warnock told CNN to describe the mood.
Democrats are facing late internal divisions, with left-wing candidates clashing at times with the party’s establishment.
In a startling display of infighting on Sunday, Democratic congresswoman Haley Stevens in Michigan endorsed Republican candidate Mike Rogers against left-wing progressive candidate Abdul El-Sayed in her state’s key Senate race.
Trump was quick to praise Stevens for her “bravery,” posting on his Truth Social platform that “Haley said what few people are willing to say.”
Stevens, who lost a bruising primary to El-Sayed in August despite being backed by the Democratic establishment, struggled to explain her decision in an interview with CNN.
“It’s just where I was at the end of the night and earlier this morning,” she said.
Trump’s Republicans have fought a political scorched-earth campaign, painting Democrats as communists and openly branding El-Sayed, who is Muslim, as a terrorist.
Addressing a crowd in Iowa on Sunday, Trump said Democrats are “extreme and dangerous radicals” who will “steal your wealth” and let in migrants to “ransack, rape and plunder.”
But polls show Americans heavily souring on Trump’s wrecking-ball act.
An NBC News poll released on Sunday showed 60 percent disapprove of his performance, particularly over high prices exacerbated by his now eight-month-long war against Iran.
While the House seems highly likely to turn Democratic, the battle for the Senate is up in the air.
Only a third of the Senate’s 100 seats are being contested in these midterms, and few of the races were seen as favorable to Democrats.
However, with surprisingly strong challenges in deeply Republican states, pollsters now say the odds of a Democratic flip are at minimum even.
The final New York Times/Siena poll released Sunday evening showed Democratic candidates leading in all seven seats viewed as most competitive, though five remained within the margin of error.
A Democratic Senate would be able to shut down Trump’s lifetime appointments to courts -- including the Supreme Court.
While Tuesday is election day, early voting has already seen a record 54 million people cast ballots around the country.
The midterms have seen about $11 billion spent on advertising, with large chunks coming from individual mega-donors.
Elon Musk, a close Trump ally who led the so-called DOGE effort in dismantling entire government departments, has given a staggering nearly half-billion dollars to help get Republicans elected.
